title: Types of Discontinuity: Removable
notes: **Definition.** f has a removable discontinuity at a when lim(x→a) f(x) = L exists and is finite, but f(a) ≠ L (including the case where f(a) is undefined).
**Worked example.** f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) equals x + 1 for x ≠ 1, so the limit at 1 is 2 while f(1) is undefined; defining f(1) = 2 removes the hole.
**Why removable.** Only one point of the graph is wrong or missing; changing that single value makes the function continuous without altering any other value.
**Contrast with a jump.** If LHL ≠ RHL, no choice of f(a) can make the function continuous, so that discontinuity is not removable.
**Common source.** Cancelling a common factor such as (x − a) from a numerator and denominator is exactly the algebraic signal of a removable hole.
**Exam caution.** After cancelling, state the restriction x ≠ a; the simplified expression describes the limit, not the original function at a.
summary: A removable discontinuity is a hole: the two-sided limit exists but f(a) is undefined or has a different value; redefining f(a) repairs it.
